Main.sentence: Donald John Trump (born June 14, 1946) is an American politician, media personality, and businessman who is the 47th ___E:president of the United States U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_the_United_States)___ .
A member of the ___E:Republican Party U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republican_Party_(United_States))___ , he served as the 45th president from 2017 to 2021.

Born into a wealthy family in New York City, Trump graduated from the ___E:University of Pennsylvania U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Pennsylvania)___ in 1968 with a ___E:bachelor's degree U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bachelor%27s_degree)___ in economics.

He became the president of his family's real estate business in 1971, renamed it ___E:the Trump Organization U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Trump_Organization)___ , and began acquiring and building skyscrapers, hotels, casinos, and golf courses.
He launched side ventures, many licensing the Trump name, and filed for six business bankruptcies in the 1990s and 2000s.
From 2004 to 2015, he hosted the reality television show The Apprentice , bolstering his fame as a billionaire.

Presenting himself as a political outsider, Trump won the ___E:2016 presidential election U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_United_States_presidential_election)___ against ___E:Democratic Party U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democratic_Party_(United_States))___ nominee ___E:Hillary Clinton U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hillary_Clinton)___ .

During his first presidency, Trump imposed ___E:a travel ban U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Executive_Order_13769)___ on seven Muslim-majority countries, expanded the ___E:Mexico–United States border wall U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mexico%E2%80%93United_States_border_wall)___ , and enforced ___E:a family separation policy U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trump_administration_family_separation_policy)___ on the border.
He rolled back environmental and business regulations, signed the ___E:Tax Cuts and Jobs Act U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tax_Cuts_and_Jobs_Act)___ , and appointed three Supreme Court justices.

In foreign policy, Trump withdrew the U.S. from agreements on climate, trade, and Iran's nuclear program, and initiated ___E:a trade war with China U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China%E2%80%93United_States_trade_war)___ .

In response to the ___E:COVID-19 pandemic U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic_in_the_United_States)___ from 2020, he downplayed its severity, contradicted health officials, and signed the ___E:CARES Act U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CARES_Act)___ .

After losing the ___E:2020 presidential election U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_presidential_election)___ to ___E:Joe Biden U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden)___ , Trump ___E:attempted to overturn the result U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Attempts_to_overturn_the_2020_United_States_presidential_election)___ , culminating in the ___E:January 6 Capitol attack U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/January_6_United_States_Capitol_attack)___ in 2021. He was impeached in 2019 for abuse of power and obstruction of Congress, and in 2021 for incitement of insurrection; the Senate acquitted him both times.

In 2023, Trump was found liable in civil cases ___E:for sexual abuse and defamation U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/E._Jean_Carroll_v._Donald_J._Trump)___ and ___E:for business fraud U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_business_fraud_lawsuit_against_the_Trump_Organization)___ .

He was found guilty ___E:of falsifying business records U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prosecution_of_Donald_Trump_in_New_York)___ in 2024, making him the first U.S. president convicted of a felony.

After winning the ___E:2024 presidential election U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_United_States_presidential_election)___ against ___E:Kamala Harris U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kamala_Harris)___ , he was sentenced to a penalty-free ___E:discharge U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discharge_(sentence))___ , and two felony indictments against him for ___E:retention of classified documents U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_prosecution_of_Donald_Trump_(classified_documents_case))___ and ___E:obstruction of the 2020 election U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_prosecution_of_Donald_Trump_(election_obstruction_case))___ were dismissed without prejudice. ___E:A racketeering case U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_election_racketeering_prosecution)___ related to the 2020 election in Georgia is pending.
Trump began his second presidency by initiating ___E:mass layoffs of federal workers U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_United_States_federal_mass_layoffs)___ .

He ___E:imposed tariffs U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tariffs_in_the_second_Trump_administration)___ on nearly all countries at the highest level since the ___E:Great Depression U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Depression)___ and signed the ___E:One Big Beautiful Bill Act U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/One_Big_Beautiful_Bill_Act)___ .

His administration's actions—including ___E:intimidation of political opponents and civil society U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Targeting_of_political_opponents_and_civil_society_under_the_second_Trump_administration)___ , deportations of immigrants, elimination of ___E:Diversity, equity, and inclusion U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diversity,_equity,_and_inclusion)___ , targeting of ___E:transgender people U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transgender)___ , and extensive use of executive orders—have drawn over 300 ___E:lawsuits challenging their legality U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Legal_affairs_of_the_second_Trump_presidency)___ .

High-profile cases have underscored his broad interpretation of the ___E:unitary executive theory U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unitary_executive_theory)___ and have led to significant conflicts with the federal courts.
Judges found many of his administration's actions to be illegal, and several have been described as unconstitutional.
Since 2015, Trump's leadership style and political agenda—often referred to as ___E:Trumpism U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trumpism)___ —have reshaped the Republican Party's identity.

Many of his comments and actions have been ___E:characterized as racist U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Racial_views_of_Donald_Trump)___ or misogynistic, and he has ___E:made false or misleading statements U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/False_or_misleading_statements_by_Donald_Trump)___ and ___E:promoted conspiracy theories U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_conspiracy_theories_promoted_by_Donald_Trump)___ to a degree unprecedented in American politics.

Trump's actions, especially in his second term, have been described as authoritarian and contributing to ___E:democratic backsliding U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democratic_backsliding_in_the_United_States)___ .

After his first term, scholars and historians ___E:ranked him U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Historical_rankings_of_presidents_of_the_United_States#Scholar_survey_summary)___ as one of the worst presidents in American history.

Donald John Trump was born on June 14, 1946, at ___E:Jamaica Hospital U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jamaica_Hospital)___ in the New York City borough of ___E:Queens U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Queens)___ , the fourth child of ___E:Fred Trump U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fred_Trump)___ and ___E:Mary Anne MacLeod Trump U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Anne_MacLeod_Trump)___ .
He is of German and Scottish descent.

He grew up with his older siblings, ___E:Maryanne U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maryanne_Trump_Barry)___ , ___E:Fred Jr. U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fred_Trump_Jr.)___ , and Elizabeth, and his younger brother, ___E:Robert U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Trump)___ , in a 23-room mansion in the ___E:Jamaica Estates U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jamaica_Estates)___ neighborhood of Queens.
Fred Trump paid his children each about $20,000 a year, equivalent to $265,000 a year in 2024. Trump was a millionaire in inflation-adjusted dollars by age eight.  [a]
Trump attended the private ___E:Kew-Forest School U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kew-Forest_School)___ through seventh grade.
He was a difficult child and showed an early interest in his father's business.
His father enrolled him in ___E:New York Military Academy U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_Military_Academy)___ , a private boarding school, to complete secondary school.
The academy pushed students into sports  and taught the imperative of winning.
In high school, he earned a ___E:B average U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grading_systems_by_country#United_States)___ .  [b]

Trump considered a show business career but instead, to be closer to home, enrolled at ___E:Fordham University U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fordham_University)___ in 1964.  He participated in the ___E:Reserve Officers' Training Corps U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reserve_Officers%27_Training_Corps)___ program during his first year, attending classes in a military uniform every Wednesday, but dropped it in his second year.  He dropped football after three or four weeks and was a mediocre squash and tennis player.

His Fordham friends introduced him to golf.  His junior year, he transferred to the ___E:Wharton School U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wharton_School)___ of the ___E:University of Pennsylvania U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Pennsylvania)___ , most often commuting to his father's office on weekends, and graduating in May 1968 with a ___E:Bachelor of Science U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bachelor_of_Science)___ in economics.

In college  he was not the top student he sometimes claimed to be.  By the time he went to Wharton—where he does not appear in a list of those receiving honors [c] —he was eyeing a career in real estate.
He was exempted from the draft during the Vietnam War due to a claim of ___E:bone spurs U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bone_spurs)___ in his heels.
Notwithstanding five years in military school,  he had no interest in going to war.
Growing up, he regarded his father and the family's pastor, ___E:Norman Vincent Peale U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norman_Vincent_Peale)___ ,  as mentors.
His father told him repeatedly that he was "a king" and to be "a killer".
Peale preached self-confidence as the impetus for prosperity.  [d]

Starting in 1968, Trump was employed at Trump Management, his father's real estate company,  which managed the middle-class apartment complexes Fred had built in ___E:Queens U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Queens)___ , ___E:Staten Island U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Staten_Island)___ , and ___E:Brooklyn U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brooklyn)___ .
His main tasks were collecting rent and making repairs  for about five years.

Captivated by its glamor and riches,  Trump asked his father to expand to ___E:Manhattan U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manhattan)___ where prices were higher, but his father was content in the outer boroughs.
In 1971, he moved to Manhattan where he planned to move the business  and commuted to his father's office.
That year, his father made himself chairman and Trump president, overseeing 48 private corporations and 15 family partnerships.
Trump began using The Trump Organization as an umbrella for the corporate names of his father's businesses.

___E:Roy Cohn U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roy_Cohn)___ , Trump's most important early influence after his father,  was his ___E:fixer U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fixer_(person))___ , lawyer, and mentor  for 13 years in the 1970s and 1980s.
Cohn taught Trump to think that life is transactional.

In 1973, Cohn helped Trump countersue the U.S. government for $100 million (equivalent to $708 million in 2024  ) over its charges that Trump's properties had discriminated against Black applicants and tenants.
Trump's counterclaims were dismissed, and the government's case was settled with the Trumps signing a consent decree agreeing to desegregate.
Four years later, the Trumps again faced the courts when they were found in contempt of the decree.
Helping Trump projects,  Cohn was a ___E:consigliere U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Consigliere)___ whose Mafia connections controlled construction unions.
In 1979, Cohn introduced political consultant ___E:Roger Stone U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roger_Stone)___ to Trump, who enlisted Stone's services to deal with the federal government.
Trump moved from his studio to a penthouse with a view and got a real estate broker's license in the mid-1970s.

Before age thirty, he showed his propensity for litigation, no matter the outcome and cost; even when he lost, he described the case as a win.  Over three decades as of 2018, Trump had been involved in more than 4,000 lawsuits,  liens, and other filings, often filed for nonpayment against him by employees, contractors, real estate brokers, and his own attorneys.

Between 1991 and 2009, Trump filed for ___E:Chapter 11 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chapter_11)___ bankruptcy protection for six of his businesses: the ___E:Plaza Hotel U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plaza_Hotel)___ in Manhattan, the casinos in ___E:Atlantic City, New Jersey U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlantic_City,_New_Jersey)___ , and the ___E:Trump Hotels & Casino Resorts U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trump_Hotels_%26_Casino_Resorts)___ company.

In 1992, Trump, his siblings Maryanne, Elizabeth, and Robert, and his cousin ___E:John W. Walter U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_W._Walter)___ formed All County Building Supply & Maintenance Corp, each with a 20 percent share.

The company had no offices and is alleged to have been a shell company for paying the vendors providing services and supplies for Trump's rental units, then billing those services and supplies to Trump Management with markups of 20–50 percent and more. The owners shared the proceeds generated by the markups.
The increased costs were used to get state approval for increasing the rents of his rent-stabilized units.
In January 1994, the siblings formed Apartment Management Associates and took over the management fees formerly collected by Trump Management.
As well as inflating rents, the schemes served to transfer assets from Fred Trump to his children and nephew and lower the tax burden.

Trump attracted public attention in 1978 with the launch of his family's first Manhattan venture: the renovation of the derelict ___E:Commodore Hotel U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Hyatt_New_York)___ , adjacent to Grand Central Terminal.

The financing was facilitated by a $400 million city property tax abatement arranged for him by his father who also, jointly with ___E:Hyatt U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hyatt)___ , guaranteed a $70 million bank construction loan.   The hotel reopened in 1980 as the ___E:Grand Hyatt Hotel U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Hyatt_New_York)___ ,  and that same year, he obtained rights to develop ___E:Trump Tower U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trump_Tower)___ , a mixed-use skyscraper in Midtown Manhattan.

The building houses the headquarters of the Trump Corporation and Trump's ___E:PAC U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Political_action_committee)___ and was his primary residence until 2019.  In 1988, Trump acquired the Plaza Hotel with a loan from a consortium of 16 banks.
The hotel filed for bankruptcy protection in 1992, and a reorganization plan was approved a month later, with the banks taking control of the property.

In 1995, Trump defaulted on over $3 billion of bank loans, and the lenders seized the Plaza Hotel along with most of his other properties in a "vast and humiliating restructuring" that allowed him to avoid personal bankruptcy.
The lead bank's attorney said of the banks' decision that they "all agreed that he'd be better alive than dead".
In 1996, Trump acquired and renovated the mostly vacant 71-story skyscraper at ___E:40 Wall Street U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/40_Wall_Street)___ , later rebranded as the Trump Building.
In the early 1990s, he won the right to develop a 70-acre (28 ha) tract in the ___E:Lincoln Square U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lincoln_Square,_Manhattan)___ neighborhood near the Hudson River.

Struggling with debt from other ventures in 1994, he sold most of his interest in the project to Asian investors, who financed the project's completion, ___E:Riverside South U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riverside_South,_Manhattan)___ .

Trump's last major construction project was the 92-story mixed-use ___E:Trump International Hotel and Tower U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trump_International_Hotel_and_Tower_(Chicago))___ in Chicago, which opened in 2008. In 2024, ___E:The New York Times and ProPublica reported U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trump_International_Hotel_and_Tower_(Chicago)#Tax_deductions)___ that the Internal Revenue Service was investigating whether he had twice written off losses incurred through construction cost overruns and lagging sales of residential units in the building he had declared to be worthless on his 2008 tax return.

In 1984, Trump opened ___E:Harrah's at Trump Plaza U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harrah%27s_at_Trump_Plaza)___ , a hotel and casino, with financing and management help from the ___E:Holiday Corporation U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holiday_Corporation)___ .
It was unprofitable, and he paid Holiday $70 million in May 1986 to take sole control.
In 1985, he bought the unopened Atlantic City Hilton Hotel and renamed it ___E:Trump's Castle U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trump%27s_Castle)___ .

Both casinos filed for ___E:Chapter 11 bankruptcy U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chapter_11_bankruptcy)___ protection in 1992.  Trump bought a third Atlantic City venue in 1988, the ___E:Trump Taj Mahal U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trump_Taj_Mahal)___ .

It was financed with $675 million in ___E:junk bonds U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Junk_bonds)___ and completed for $1.1 billion, opening in April 1990.  He filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection in 1991. Under the provisions of the restructuring agreement, he gave up half his initial stake and personally guaranteed future performance.

To reduce his $900 million of personal debt, he sold the ___E:Trump Shuttle U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trump_Shuttle)___ airline; his megayacht, the Trump Princess , which had been leased to his casinos and kept docked; and other businesses.
In 1995, Trump founded Trump Hotels & Casino Resorts (THCR), which assumed ownership of the Trump Plaza.
THCR purchased the Taj Mahal and the Trump Castle in 1996 and went bankrupt in 2004 and 2009, leaving him with 10 percent ownership.
He remained chairman until 2009.
In 1985, Trump acquired the ___E:Mar-a-Lago U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mar-a-Lago)___ estate in Palm Beach, Florida.
In 1995, he converted the estate into a private club with an initiation fee and annual dues. He continued to use a wing of the house as a private residence.
He declared the club his primary residence in 2019.  He began ___E:building and buying golf courses U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Trump_and_golf)___ in 1999, owning 17 golf courses by 2016.
The Trump Organization often licensed the Trump name for consumer products and services, including foodstuffs, apparel, learning courses, and home furnishings.
Over 50 licensing or management deals involved Trump's name, generating at least $59 million for his companies.
By 2018, only two consumer goods companies continued to license his name.  During the 2000s, Trump licensed his name to residential property developments worldwide, 40 of which were never built.
In 1970, Trump invested $70,000 of his father's wealth to receive billing as coproducer of a Broadway comedy—and lost the money.

After making low-ball bids for the ___E:New York Mets U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_Mets)___ and the ___E:Cleveland Indians U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cleveland_Indians)___ baseball teams, in 1983 for about $6 million, he purchased the ___E:New Jersey Generals U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Jersey_Generals)___ , a team in the ___E:United States Football League U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Football_League)___ .

The league folded after the 1985 season, largely due to his attempt to move to a fall schedule (when it would have competed with the ___E:National Football League U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Football_League)___ for audience) and his attempt to force a merger with the NFL by bringing an antitrust suit.  Trump and his Plaza Hotel hosted several boxing matches at the ___E:Atlantic City Convention Hall U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlantic_City_Convention_Hall)___ .

In 1989 and 1990, he lent his name to the ___E:Tour de Trump U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tour_de_Trump)___ cycling stage race, an attempt to create an American equivalent of European races such as the ___E:Tour de France U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tour_de_France)___ or the ___E:Giro d'Italia U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giro_d%27Italia)___ .

From 1986 to 1988, he purchased significant blocks of shares in various public companies while suggesting that he intended to take over the company and then sold his shares for a profit,  leading some observers to think he was engaged in ___E:greenmail U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greenmail)___ .
The New York Times found that he initially made millions of dollars in such stock transactions, but "lost most, if not all, of those gains after investors stopped taking his takeover talk seriously".

In 1988, Trump purchased the ___E:Eastern Air Lines Shuttle U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastern_Air_Lines_Shuttle)___ , financing the purchase with $380 million (equivalent to $1.01 billion in 2024  ) in loans from a syndicate of 22 banks.
He renamed the airline ___E:Trump Shuttle U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trump_Shuttle)___ and operated it until 1992.  He defaulted on his loans in 1991, and ownership passed to the banks.

In 1996, he purchased the ___E:Miss Universe U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miss_Universe)___ pageants, including ___E:Miss USA U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miss_USA)___ and ___E:Miss Teen USA U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miss_Teen_USA)___ .

Due to disagreements with CBS about scheduling, he took both pageants to NBC in 2002.   In 2007, he received a star on the ___E:Hollywood Walk of Fame U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hollywood_Walk_of_Fame)___ for his work as producer of Miss Universe.
NBC and Univision dropped the pageants in June 2015 in reaction to his comments about Mexican immigrants.

In 2005, Trump cofounded ___E:Trump University U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trump_University)___ , a company that sold real estate seminars for up to $35,000. After New York State authorities notified the company that its use of "university" violated state law (as it was not an academic institution), its name was changed to the Trump Entrepreneur Initiative in 2010.  In 2013, the State of New York filed a $40 million civil suit against Trump University, alleging that the company made false statements and defrauded consumers.
Additionally, two class actions were filed in federal court against Trump and his companies.
Internal documents revealed that employees were instructed to use a hard-sell approach, and former employees testified that Trump University had defrauded or lied to its students.
Shortly after he won the 2016 presidential election, he agreed to pay a total of $25 million to settle the three cases.

The Donald J. Trump Foundation was a ___E:private foundation U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Private_foundation_(United_States))___ established in 1988.  From 1987 to 2006, Trump gave his foundation $5.4 million, which had been spent by the end of 2006. After donating a total of $65,000 in 2007–2008, he stopped donating any personal funds to the charity,  which received millions from other donors, including $5 million from ___E:Vince McMahon U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vince_McMahon)___ .
The foundation gave to health- and sports-related charities, conservative groups,  and charities that held events at Trump properties.

In 2016, The Washington Post reported that the charity had committed several potential legal and ethical violations, including self-dealing and ___E:tax evasion U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tax_evasion)___ .

Also in 2016, the New York attorney general stated the foundation had violated state law by soliciting donations without submitting to required annual external audits and ordered it to cease its fundraising activities in New York immediately.
Trump's team announced in December 2016 that the foundation would be dissolved.
In June 2018, the New York attorney general's office filed a civil suit against the foundation, Trump, and his adult children, seeking $2.8 million in restitution and additional penalties.
In December 2018, the foundation ceased operation and disbursed its assets to other charities.
In November 2019, a New York state judge ordered Trump to pay $2 million to a group of charities for misusing the foundation's funds, in part to finance his presidential campaign.
According to a review of state and federal court files conducted by USA Today in 2018, Trump and his businesses had been involved in more than 4,000 state and federal legal actions.

While he has not filed for ___E:personal bankruptcy U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Personal_bankruptcy)___ , his over-leveraged hotel and casino businesses in Atlantic City and New York filed for ___E:Chapter 11 bankruptcy U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chapter_11_bankruptcy)___ protection six times between 1991 and 2009.  They continued to operate while the banks restructured debt and reduced his shares in the properties.
During the 1980s, more than 70 banks had lent Trump $4 billion.

After his corporate bankruptcies of the early 1990s, most major banks, with the exception of ___E:Deutsche Bank U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deutsche_Bank)___ , declined to lend to him.  After the ___E:January 6 Capitol attack U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/January_6_United_States_Capitol_attack)___ , the bank decided not to do business with him or his affiliated company in the future.
